arXiv:2610.24631v1 [math.CO] 17 Oct 2026

Random Tournaments Are Asymptotically Almost Surely Link-irregular

Lily Zhang ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Berkeley. Email address: pink@berkeley.edu.
October 17, 2026
Abstract

Bastien and Khormali (2025) conjectured that a nontrivial link-irregular tournament with nn vertices exists if and only if n≥6n\geq 6. Their work establishes the conjecture for n≤100n\leq 100. We present a probabilistic argument for the existence of link-irregular tournaments with nn vertices when n≥9n\geq 9 to resolve the conjecture. In fact, we show that a random tournament is asymptotically almost surely link-irregular.

Keywords: Link-irregular digraphs, directed graphs, random tournaments, probabilistic method.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C20, 05D40, 05C80.

1 Introduction

The study of links of graphs was first introduced by Ali, Chartrand, and Zhang [1]. This study has since been extended to links of directed graphs by Bastien and Khormali [2]. However, for the practical purposes of this paper, we assert the definitions involving link for directed graphs only.

Given a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) of a directed graph, we denote its neighborhood (set of in-neighbors and out-neighbors) by N⁡(v)N(v). The link of a vertex v∈Gv\in G is defined by

L⁡(v)=G⁡[N⁡(v)].L(v)=G[N(v)].

In other words, L⁡(v)L(v) is the subgraph formed by the neighborhood of v∈Gv\in G. GG is link-irregular if for all distinct u,v∈Gu,v\in G,

L⁡(u)≇L⁡(v).L(u)\not\cong L(v).

It’s easy to see that link-irregular tournaments are directed graphs TT which satisfy for all distinct u,v∈V⁡(T)u,v\in V(T):

T−u≇T−v.T-u\not\cong T-v.

Bastien and Khormali have conjectured that nontrivial link-irregular tournaments with nn vertices exist if and only if n≥6n\geq 6. They prove that the conjecture holds up to n=100n=100 [2].

In what follows, we resolve the conjecture by proving that link-irregular tournaments with nn vertices exist when n≥9n\geq 9. Our work invokes a probabilistic argument, which does not provide explicit examples of such directed graphs. However, the robustness of probabilistic reasoning provides us with a proof that uniformly random tournaments with nn vertices are asymptotically almost surely link-irregular.

Both of the main results have been formalized in the Lean 4 proof assistant and are available on GitHub [5].

3 Proof of Existence

Our goal is to prove that if n≥9n\geq 9, then there exists a link-irregular tournament with nn vertices, whence the conjecture follows from the facts we mentioned in the introduction. We do this via Theorem 6, which additionally shows that random tournaments are asymptotically almost surely link-irregular.

There is notation that we wish to introduce that’s only applicable for Lemma 2 and Theorem 3.

Given distinct u,v∈{1,…,n}u,v\in\{1,\dotsc,n\} and a bijection

φ:{1,…,n}∖{u}→{1,…,n}∖{v},\varphi\colon\{1,\dotsc,n\}\setminus\{u\}\to\{1,\dotsc,n\}\setminus\{v\},

define the event

Bφ={φ​ is an isomorphism from ​Tn−u​ to ​Tn−v}.B_{\varphi}=\{\varphi\text{ is an isomorphism from }T_{n}-u\text{ to }T_{n}-v\}.

For every x≠ux\not=u, draw the directed edge x⟶φ⁡(x)x\longrightarrow\varphi(x). Using the convention that loops x⟶xx\longrightarrow x are directed cycles of length 11, let CφC_{\varphi} be the set of vertices on directed cycles, and define σφ:Cφ→Cφ\sigma_{\varphi}\colon C_{\varphi}\to C_{\varphi} via σφ​(x)=φ​(x)\sigma_{\varphi}(x)=\varphi(x).

Lemma 2.

Let n≥2n\geq 2 be an integer, let u,v∈{1,…,n}u,v\in\{1,\dotsc,n\} be distinct, and let
φ:{1,…,n}∖{u}→{1,…,n}∖{v}\varphi\colon\{1,\dotsc,n\}\setminus\{u\}\to\{1,\dotsc,n\}\setminus\{v\} be a bijection. Then

ℙ⁡(Bφ)≤2−(n−12)+o2​(σφ).\mathbb{P}(B_{\varphi})\leq 2^{-\binom{n-1}{2}+o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})}.
Proof.

Let DφD_{\varphi} be the directed graph whose vertices are V⁡(Dφ)=({1,…,n}2)V(D_{\varphi})=\binom{\{1,\dotsc,n\}}{2}, and the (n−12)\binom{n-1}{2} directed edges are

{x,y}⟶{φ⁡(x),φ⁡(y)}\{x,y\}\longrightarrow\{\varphi(x),\varphi(y)\}

where x,y≠ux,y\not=u.

A vertex {x,y}∈V⁡(Dφ)\{x,y\}\in V(D_{\varphi}) lies on a directed cycle if and only if x,y∈Cφx,y\in C_{\varphi}, indicating that the directed cycles of DφD_{\varphi} are precisely the orbits of f:(Cφ2)→(Cφ2)f:\binom{C_{\varphi}}{2}\to\binom{C_{\varphi}}{2} by

f⁡({x,y})={σφ​(x),σφ​(y)}.f(\{x,y\})=\{\sigma_{\varphi}(x),\sigma_{\varphi}(y)\}.

So there are o2​(σφ)o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi}) connected components that are directed cycles.

Since φ\varphi is a bijection, each vertex {x,y}∈V⁡(Dφ)\{x,y\}\in V(D_{\varphi}) satisfies
deg−⁡({x,y}),deg+⁡({x,y})≤1\deg^{-}(\{x,y\}),\deg^{+}(\{x,y\})\leq 1. So every connected component of DφD_{\varphi} is either a directed path or a directed cycle. Therefore the amount of connected components of DφD_{\varphi} is

r=|V⁡(Dφ)|−|E⁡(Dφ)|+o2​(σφ)=(n2)−(n−12)+o2​(σφ).r=\left\lvert V(D_{\varphi})\right\rvert-\left\lvert E(D_{\varphi})\right\rvert+o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})=\binom{n}{2}-\binom{n-1}{2}+o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi}).

Assuming BφB_{\varphi} occurs, the orientation of one unordered pair in TnT_{n} determines the orientations of all unordered pairs within this connected component. We conclude at most 2r2^{r} tournaments for which BφB_{\varphi} occurs, thus

ℙ⁡(Bφ)≤2r2(n2)=2(n2)−(n−12)+o2​(σφ)2(n2)=2−(n−12)+o2​(σφ),\mathbb{P}(B_{\varphi})\leq\frac{2^{r}}{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}=\frac{2^{\binom{n}{2}-\binom{n-1}{2}+o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})}}{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}=2^{-\binom{n-1}{2}+o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})},

exactly as desired. ∎

Theorem 3.

Let n≥2n\geq 2 be an integer. Let u,v∈{1,…,n}u,v\in\{1,\dotsc,n\} be distinct. Then

ℙ(Tn−u≅Tn−v)≤(n−2)!⋅2−(n−12)∑k=0n−2gk.\mathbb{P}(T_{n}-u\cong T_{n}-v)\leq(n-2)!\cdot 2^{-\binom{n-1}{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}g_{k}.
Proof.

Taking the union over all bijections
φ:{1,…,n}∖{u}→{1,…,n}∖{v}\varphi:\{1,\dotsc,n\}\setminus\{u\}\to\{1,\dotsc,n\}\setminus\{v\} gives the equality of events

{Tn−u≅Tn−v}=⋃φBφ.\{T_{n}-u\cong T_{n}-v\}=\bigcup_{\varphi}B_{\varphi}.

ℙ⁡(Tn−u≅Tn−v)≤∑φℙ⁡(Bφ)≤2−(n−12)​∑φ2o2​(σφ).\mathbb{P}(T_{n}-u\cong T_{n}-v)\leq\sum_{\varphi}\mathbb{P}(B_{\varphi})\leq 2^{-\binom{n-1}{2}}\sum_{\varphi}2^{o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})}.

Our goal is to prove the sufficient inequality

∑φ2o2​(σφ)≤(n−2)!⋅∑k=0n−2gk.\sum_{\varphi}2^{o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})}\leq(n-2)!\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}g_{k}.

∑φ|Cφ|=k2o2​(σφ).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\varphi\\ \left\lvert C_{\varphi}\right\rvert=k\end{subarray}}2^{o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})}.
  • •

    There are (n−2k)\binom{n-2}{k} ways to choose the kk vertices out of the n−2n-2 vertices that aren’t u,vu,v to determine CφC_{\varphi}.

  • •

    For a fixed C∈({1,…,n}∖{u,v}k)C\in\binom{\{1,\dotsc,n\}\setminus\{u,v\}}{k} and permutation σ:C→C\sigma:C\to C, there are (n−k−2)!(n-k-2)! ways to order the remaining n−k−2n-k-2 vertices to form the directed path from vv to uu. So there are (n−k−2)!(n-k-2)! bijections φ\varphi with Cφ=CC_{\varphi}=C, σφ=σ\sigma_{\varphi}=\sigma.

  • •

    For a fixed CφC_{\varphi}, summing 2o2​(σφ)2^{o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})} over all permutations of CφC_{\varphi} yields

    ∑σ∈Sym⁡(Cφ)2o2​(σ)=∑σ∈Sk2o2​(σ).\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(C_{\varphi})}2^{o_{2}(\sigma)}=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}2^{o_{2}(\sigma)}.

Taking the sum from k=0k=0 to n−2n-2, we obtain

∑φ2o2​(σφ)\displaystyle\sum_{\varphi}2^{o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})} =∑k=0n−2∑φ|Cφ|=k2o2​(σφ)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\varphi\\ \left\lvert C_{\varphi}\right\rvert=k\end{subarray}}2^{o_{2}(\sigma_{\varphi})}
=∑k=0n−2(n−2k)⋅(n−k−2)!⋅∑σ∈Sk2o2​(σ)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}\binom{n-2}{k}\cdot(n-k-2)!\cdot\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}2^{o_{2}(\sigma)}
=∑k=0n−2(n−2k)⋅(n−k−2)!⋅k!⋅gk\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}\binom{n-2}{k}\cdot(n-k-2)!\cdot k!\cdot g_{k}
=(n−2)!⋅∑k=0n−2gk,\displaystyle=(n-2)!\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}g_{k},

Lemma 4.

Let n≥8n\geq 8 be an integer. Then

gn<2⋅2(n2)n!.g_{n}<2\cdot\frac{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}{n!}.
Proof.

Buhrman, Li, Tromp, and Vitányi [3, Corollary 2] already supply the asymptotically stronger

gn≤2(n2)n!​(1+4​n42n).g_{n}\leq\frac{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}{n!}\left(1+\frac{4n^{4}}{2^{n}}\right).

We merely show that 2n>4​n42^{n}>4n^{4} for n≥19n\geq 19 via induction, then we perform a finite check on n∈[8,18]n\in[8,18].

Base case (n=19n=19): 219=524288>521284=4⋅1942^{19}=524288>521284=4\cdot 19^{4}.

2>n4(n−1)4.2>\frac{n^{4}}{(n-1)^{4}}.

This is true since the fourth root of the right side is

nn−1≤2019<1.18<24.\frac{n}{n-1}\leq\frac{20}{19}<1.18<\sqrt[4]{2}.

Lemma 5.

Let n≥7n\geq 7 be an integer. Then

∑k=0ngk<4⋅2(n2)n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}g_{k}<4\cdot\frac{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}{n!}
Proof.

We show this via induction on nn.

Base case (n=7n=7): Just compare

g0+⋯+g7=1+1+2\displaystyle g_{0}+\dotsb+g_{7}=1+1+2 +4+11+34+156+1044=1253.\displaystyle+4+11+34+156+1044=1253.
4⋅2(72)7!\displaystyle 4\cdot\frac{2^{\binom{7}{2}}}{7!} =2235040=1664+128315.\displaystyle=\frac{2^{23}}{5040}=1664+\frac{128}{315}.

Induction step: Assuming it true for n−1n-1, we derive using Lemma 4 that

∑k=0ngk<4⋅2(n−12)(n−1)!+2⋅2(n2)n!.\sum_{k=0}^{n}g_{k}<4\cdot\frac{2^{\binom{n-1}{2}}}{(n-1)!}+2\cdot\frac{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}{n!}.

It’s enough to show

2⋅2(n−12)(n−1)!≤2(n2)n!,2\cdot\frac{2^{\binom{n-1}{2}}}{(n-1)!}\leq\frac{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}{n!},

where division reduces this to

2n⁡(n−1)−(n−1)​(n−2)2n=2n−1n≥2.\frac{2^{\frac{n(n-1)-(n-1)(n-2)}{2}}}{n}=\frac{2^{n-1}}{n}\geq 2.

Obviously this is true for n≥8n\geq 8. ∎

Theorem 6.

If n≥9n\geq 9 is an integer, then there exists a link-irregular tournament with nn vertices. In fact, TnT_{n} is asymptotically almost surely link-irregular.

Proof.

Let u,v∈{1,…,n}u,v\in\{1,\dotsc,n\} be distinct.

If n−2≥8n-2\geq 8, combining Theorem 3 and Lemma 5 results in the chain of inequalities

ℙ⁡(Tn−u≅Tn−v)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(T_{n}-u\cong T_{n}-v) ≤(n−2)!⋅2−(n−12)∑k=0n−2gk\displaystyle\leq(n-2)!\cdot 2^{-\binom{n-1}{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}g_{k}
<(n−2)!⋅2−(n−12)⋅4⋅2(n−22)(n−2)!\displaystyle<(n-2)!\cdot 2^{-\binom{n-1}{2}}\cdot 4\cdot\frac{2^{\binom{n-2}{2}}}{(n-2)!}
=4⋅2(n−2)​(n−3)−(n−1)​(n−2)2\displaystyle=4\cdot 2^{\frac{(n-2)(n-3)-(n-1)(n-2)}{2}}
=2−n+4.\displaystyle=2^{-n+4}.

Taking the union bound over all (n2)\binom{n}{2} unordered pairs u≠vu\not=v of {1,…,n}\{1,\dotsc,n\}, we derive

ℙ⁡(Tn​ is not link-irregular)<(n2)⋅2−n+4⏟an​⟶n→∞​ 0.\mathbb{P}(T_{n}\text{ is not link-irregular})<\underbrace{\binom{n}{2}\cdot 2^{-n+4}}_{a_{n}}\;\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\;0.

This gives us the second part of the theorem.

It’s not hard to show that ana_{n} is decreasing in nn, and also

a10=(102)⋅2−10+4=4564<1.a_{10}=\binom{10}{2}\cdot 2^{-10+4}=\frac{45}{64}<1.

Hence the first part of the theorem for n≥10n\geq 10.

We handle the n=9n=9 case separately, which follows via directly applying a similar union bound and Theorem 3:

ℙ⁡(T9​ is not link-irregular)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(T_{9}\text{ is not link-irregular}) ≤(92)⋅7!⋅2−(82)​(g0+⋯+g7)\displaystyle\leq\binom{9}{2}\cdot 7!\cdot 2^{-\binom{8}{2}}(g_{0}+\dotsb+g_{7})
=36⋅7!⋅1253228\displaystyle=\frac{36\cdot 7!\cdot 1253}{2^{28}}
=35522554194304\displaystyle=\frac{3552255}{4194304}
<1.\displaystyle<1.

∎
